LONDON, England -- Painfully hot, they make your eyes water, your heart race and can turn your face embarrassingly red. Chilies have been used for many millenia both for their medicinal benefits and exciting falvor. Once only a staple of cuisine from far flung regions of the world, chilies can now be found in almost any dish around the globe. Last week an Indian woman wolfed down 51 "ghost chilies," -- the world's spiciest -- in two minutes and smeared the seeds on her eyes for an entry into the Guinness World Records. Anandita Dutta Tamuly, 28, achieved the bizarre and fiery undertaking in the Indian north-eastern state of Assam. She was cheered on by British chef Gordon Ramsay, who also attempted a bite of the hot stuff before begging for water. A single seed can cause watering eyes, as well as a burning sensation in the mouth that can last up to five hours. A chili's spiciness is measured in Scoville units; the number of times a chili extract must be diluted in water in order for it to lose its heat. The "ghost chili", also known as bhut jolokia, has more than 1 million Scoville units, while Tabasco sauce ranges from 2,500 to 5,000 Scoville units and jalapeno peppers from 2,500 to 8,000 units. Chilies have formed part of the diet in the Americas since approximately 7,500 BC and owe most of their fame to their sometimes unbearably spicy flavor. But they have also long been recognized for their health benefits. Scientific research --and legend--  have attributed health wonders to chilies over the years. Diego Alvarez Chanca, a physician on explorer Christopher Columbus' second voyage to the West Indies in 1493, first wrote about the pepper's medicinal effects back in 1494. Below we look at effects eating chilies has on the body. Skin . Other than for its flavor-enhancing qualities, chili is, oddly enough, used to fight the summer heat. As the chili causes extreme sweating and blood rushing to the face, it cools the body down when the sweat evaporates, making it useful for combating heat. These same heat inducing properties are said to have a cumulative effect and over time are believed to alleviate pain when used in treatments for anything from arthritis and psoriasis to shingles and severe burns. Brain . The substances that give chili peppers their intensity when eaten or applied on the skin are called capsaicinoids. When consumed, capsaicinoids connect with pain receptors in the mouth and throat that are normally responsible for sensing heat. Once activated by the capsaicinoids, these receptors send a message to the brain that the person has consumed something hot. The brain responds to the burning sensation by raising the heart rate, increasing perspiration and releasing endorphins, called the body's "natural painkillers" and "happy hormones." Stomach . Chilies have long been associated with soothing the digestive system, by acting as stomach cleansers. According to the UK Food Guide, chili helps to settle stomach upset and encourages the production of good digestive acid. Chili aficionados believe the fruits can also induce weight loss because the substance that makes them "hot" speed up the body's metabolism. However, one study by the American Institute of Cancer Research performed in Mexico showed in 2003 that a high consumption of chilies (approximately nine to 25 jalapeno peppers per day) is in fact associated with stomach cancer. Immune system . Red chilies contain high amounts of carotene and vitamin C. It is said that chilies contain more vitamin C than citrus fruits. Chili peppers are also a good source of vitamin B6 and are very high in potassium, magnesium and iron, giving them a reputation for naturally boosting the body's immune system. Heart and other cardiovascular effects . A 2006 study published in the British Journal of Nutrition showed that after adding chili to the diet, bad cholesterol, that can often lead to heart problems, took a longer time to develop into heart diseases.

outputs.L1:
**LONDON, England —** Painfully hot, chilies can make your eyes water, your heart race, and your face turn an embarrassing shade of red. They have been used for millennia for both their medicinal benefits and their exciting flavor.

Once a staple only in cuisines from far-flung regions of the world, chilies can now be found in almost any dish around the globe.

Last week, a 28-year-old Indian woman, Anandita Dutta Tamuly, devoured 51 “ghost chilies”—the world’s spiciest—in two minutes and rubbed the seeds into her eyes as part of an attempt to enter Guinness World Records. She completed the bizarre and fiery feat in the northeastern Indian state of Assam.

British chef Gordon Ramsay cheered her on and also attempted a bite of the fiery pepper before begging for water.

A single seed can cause watering eyes and a burning sensation in the mouth that may last for up to five hours.

A chili’s spiciness is measured in Scoville units, which indicate the number of times a chili extract must be diluted in water before it loses its heat. The “ghost chili,” also known as *bhut jolokia*, has more than 1 million Scoville units, while Tabasco sauce ranges from 2,500 to 5,000 Scoville units and jalapeño peppers from 2,500 to 8,000 units.

Chilies have formed part of the diet in the Americas since approximately 7,500 BC and owe much of their fame to their sometimes unbearably spicy flavor. However, they have also long been recognized for their health benefits.

Over the years, both scientific research and legend have attributed remarkable health effects to chilies. Diego Alvarez Chanca, a physician on explorer Christopher Columbus’ second voyage to the West Indies in 1493, first wrote about the pepper’s medicinal effects in 1494.

Below, we examine the effects that eating chilies can have on the body.

**Skin**

In addition to their flavor-enhancing qualities, chilies are, oddly enough, used to combat the summer heat. By causing extreme perspiration and a rush of blood to the face, chilies help cool the body as sweat evaporates.

These same heat-inducing properties are said to have a cumulative effect and, over time, are believed to alleviate pain when used in treatments for conditions ranging from arthritis and psoriasis to shingles and severe burns.

**Brain**

The substances that give chili peppers their intensity when eaten or applied to the skin are called capsaicinoids.

When consumed, capsaicinoids bind to pain receptors in the mouth and throat that are normally responsible for sensing heat. Once activated, these receptors send a message to the brain indicating that the person has consumed something hot.

The brain responds to the burning sensation by raising the heart rate, increasing perspiration, and releasing endorphins—often described as the body’s “natural painkillers” and “happy hormones.”

**Stomach**

Chilies have long been associated with soothing the digestive system by acting as stomach cleansers. According to the UK Food Guide, chili helps settle an upset stomach and encourages the production of beneficial digestive acid.

Chili aficionados also believe that the fruits can promote weight loss because the substance that makes them “hot” speeds up the body’s metabolism.

However, a 2003 study conducted in Mexico by the American Institute for Cancer Research found that high chili consumption—approximately nine to 25 jalapeño peppers per day—was associated with stomach cancer.

**Immune system**

Red chilies contain high levels of carotene and vitamin C. They are said to contain more vitamin C than citrus fruits.

Chili peppers are also a good source of vitamin B6 and are rich in potassium, magnesium, and iron, giving them a reputation for naturally boosting the body’s immune system.

**Heart and other cardiovascular effects**

A 2006 study published in the *British Journal of Nutrition* found that, after chili was added to the diet, “bad” cholesterol—which can often lead to heart problems—took longer to develop into heart disease.

The ghost chili, or *bhut jolokia*, measures more than 1 million Scoville units. By comparison, Tabasco sauce is rated between 2,500 and 5,000 units, while jalapeño peppers range from 2,500 to 8,000.

Chilies have been eaten in the Americas since about 7,500 BC. Although they are best known for a flavor that can sometimes be almost intolerably hot, they have also been valued for their perceived health benefits.

Over the centuries, both scientific studies and folklore have credited chilies with remarkable medicinal properties. In 1494, Diego Alvarez Chanca—a doctor who accompanied explorer Christopher Columbus on his second journey to the West Indies in 1493—became the first person to write about the pepper’s medical effects.

Below are some of the ways eating chilies may affect the body.

### Skin

Strangely, despite their fiery taste, chilies are used to help people cope with summer heat. They trigger heavy sweating and increase blood flow to the face. As the sweat evaporates, it lowers the body’s temperature, which can make chilies useful in hot conditions.

These heat-producing effects are also said to build up over time and reduce pain. Chili-based treatments have been used for conditions ranging from arthritis, psoriasis, and shingles to serious burns.

### Brain

Capsaicinoids are the compounds responsible for the powerful sensation created when chilies are eaten or placed on the skin. After consumption, these substances attach to pain receptors in the mouth and throat that normally detect heat.

The activated receptors then tell the brain that something hot has entered the body. In response to the burning feeling, the brain speeds up the heart rate, causes greater sweating, and releases endorphins—chemicals often described as the body’s “natural painkillers” and “happy hormones.”

### Stomach

Chilies have traditionally been linked to improved digestion and are sometimes regarded as stomach cleansers. The UK Food Guide says chili may calm an upset stomach and stimulate the production of beneficial digestive acid.

Chili enthusiasts also claim the fruit can help with weight loss because the chemical responsible for its heat accelerates metabolism. However, a 2003 study conducted in Mexico by the American Institute for Cancer Research found that eating large quantities of chilies—roughly nine to 25 jalapeño peppers each day—was associated with stomach cancer.

### Immune system

Red chilies contain substantial amounts of carotene and vitamin C. They are said to provide more vitamin C than citrus fruit. They are also a good source of vitamin B6 and contain high levels of potassium, magnesium, and iron. These nutrients have helped give chilies a reputation for naturally strengthening the immune system.

### Heart and other cardiovascular effects

A study published in the *British Journal of Nutrition* in 2006 found that, when chili was added to the diet, “bad” cholesterol—which can contribute to heart problems—took longer to progress into heart disease.

### The Power of Chilies

Chilies are valued around the world for both their intense flavor and their reputation as medicinal plants. For centuries, people have used them not only to season food but also in traditional remedies. Historical evidence suggests that chilies were cultivated in the Americas thousands of years ago before spreading to Europe, Asia, and Africa. Today, they are essential ingredients in many cuisines and continue to attract scientific interest because of their possible effects on pain, circulation, metabolism, and body temperature.

The burning sensation produced by chilies comes mainly from capsaicin, a chemical concentrated in the inner tissue surrounding the seeds. Capsaicin activates receptors that normally detect potentially harmful heat. Although a chili does not actually burn the mouth, the nervous system responds as if it has encountered something dangerously hot. This reaction can cause severe burning, watering eyes, a runny nose, facial flushing, a faster heart rate, and heavy sweating. Particularly powerful chilies may also lead to coughing, nausea, or stomach discomfort.

The intensity of a chili is commonly measured in Scoville Heat Units. Developed by pharmacist Wilbur Scoville, the Scoville scale originally measured how much a chili extract had to be diluted before its heat could no longer be detected. Modern laboratories can determine heat more accurately by measuring the concentration of capsaicinoids. Mild peppers rank low on the scale, while exceptionally hot varieties can reach hundreds of thousands or even millions of Scoville units.

One of the most famous extremely hot varieties is the Bhut Jolokia, commonly known as the “ghost chili.” Its extraordinary power was demonstrated by Anandita Dutta Tamuly, who achieved international attention by consuming 51 ghost chilies in a record-breaking performance. Her feat highlighted both the remarkable heat of the peppers and the wide differences in people’s tolerance for capsaicin. For most individuals, eating even one ghost chili can produce an overwhelming physical response.

Despite the discomfort they cause, chilies may have useful effects. When capsaicin activates heat-sensitive receptors, the body attempts to cool itself by producing sweat. As that sweat evaporates from the skin, it removes heat and may help reduce body temperature. This process may partly explain why spicy foods are especially popular in many hot climates.

Scientific research has also explored capsaicin’s potential health applications. It is used in some topical creams and patches intended to relieve certain forms of pain by altering the activity of pain-sensitive nerves. Researchers have examined whether chili consumption might influence metabolism, cardiovascular health, and inflammation, although such findings should not be treated as proof that chilies can prevent or cure disease. Their effects depend on the amount consumed, the individual’s tolerance, and existing medical conditions.

Chilies therefore occupy an unusual position between food, physical challenge, and medicine. They can provoke dramatic reactions—including burning pain, tears, a rapid heartbeat, flushing, and sweating—yet the same chemical responsible for these sensations may also have therapeutic value. From their long history of cultivation to scientific measurements of heat and Tamuly’s extraordinary consumption of 51 ghost chilies, chilies demonstrate how a small fruit can exert a powerful influence on the human body.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style health feature explaining what happens to the body when you eat chili peppers, including effects on the skin, brain, stomach, immune system, and heart.
counterfactuals.output:
# Feel the burn: What happens to your body when you eat chili peppers

**That fiery bite can trigger sweating, a rush of feel-good chemicals and changes throughout the digestive and cardiovascular systems. But spicy food isn’t for everyone.**

The heat of a chili pepper isn’t actually burning your mouth. It’s a chemical illusion created largely by **capsaicin**, a compound concentrated in the pepper’s white inner ribs.

Capsaicin activates **TRPV1 receptors**, nerve sensors that normally respond to potentially harmful heat. The brain interprets the signal as “hot,” setting off reactions across the body — even though the temperature of your food may be perfectly safe.

Here’s what may happen next.

## Skin: Flushing, sweating and a runny nose

Once heat-sensitive nerves are activated, the body tries to cool itself. Blood vessels near the skin widen, which can make the face look red or flushed, and sweat glands switch on.

Sweating after spicy food — known as **gustatory sweating** — often affects the forehead, scalp and upper lip. Capsaicin can also stimulate nerves in the nose, producing watery eyes or a runny nose.

Touching hot peppers may irritate the skin, and transferring capsaicin to the eyes can cause intense pain. Gloves can help when handling very hot varieties. If exposure occurs, washing with dish soap may remove the oily compound more effectively than water alone.

## Brain: Pain signals followed by pleasure

Capsaicin sends a warning signal to the brain, which may respond by releasing pain-modulating chemicals such as **endorphins**. Dopamine and other reward pathways may also contribute to the exhilaration some people describe as a “spicy food high.”

Repeated exposure can temporarily desensitize TRPV1 receptors, helping explain why regular chili eaters often build tolerance. That same effect is used medically: Topical capsaicin creams and patches can reduce certain types of nerve and arthritis pain after an initial burning sensation.

Capsaicin is not physically addictive in the way nicotine or opioids can be, but people may come to enjoy — and seek out — the combination of excitement, pain and relief.

## Stomach and intestines: More activity, and sometimes discomfort

Spicy foods do not cause most stomach ulcers. The leading causes are infection with *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria and frequent use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen.

However, capsaicin can aggravate symptoms in some people. It may cause abdominal pain, nausea, cramping or diarrhea, especially in large amounts or among those who aren’t accustomed to it. It can also worsen heartburn in people with gastroesophageal reflux disease, although responses vary.

The infamous “second burn” during a bowel movement occurs because capsaicin may remain active as it travels through the digestive tract, stimulating similar heat-sensitive receptors at the other end.

Milk or yogurt can be more soothing than water because the milk protein casein helps lift capsaicin away from receptors. High-fat foods may also help dissolve it.

## Immune system: Helpful nutrients, but no magic shield

Chili peppers supply **vitamin C, vitamin A precursors and antioxidant plant compounds**. These nutrients support normal immune function and help protect cells from oxidative damage.

Laboratory research suggests capsaicin can influence inflammation and immune signaling, but the effects are complex. Eating chili peppers has not been proved to “boost” immunity or prevent infections in humans.

How peppers are prepared matters, too. A small amount of fresh chili can add nutrients and flavor, while heavily salted hot sauces or spicy processed foods may come with large amounts of sodium.

## Heart: A temporary workout, with possible long-term benefits

A spicy meal can briefly increase heart rate, widen blood vessels and create a sensation of warmth. Capsaicin may also modestly affect metabolism and blood-vessel function.

Several observational studies have linked regular chili consumption with lower rates of cardiovascular death or overall mortality. But those studies cannot prove that peppers are responsible. Chili eaters may differ in diet, activity, income or other health behaviors, and researchers have not established an ideal dose.

Chili peppers should not be viewed as a substitute for proven heart-protective habits such as exercising, avoiding tobacco, sleeping adequately and eating a diet rich in vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains.

## When the heat becomes too much

For most healthy adults, culinary amounts of chili are safe. Very large doses — particularly in extreme food challenges or concentrated extracts — can cause severe vomiting, intense abdominal pain, blood-pressure changes and, rarely, serious complications.

Seek medical attention for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, persistent vomiting, severe headache or abdominal pain that does not improve.

The bottom line: If chili peppers agree with you, they can be a flavorful, nutrient-rich part of a balanced diet. The burn is mostly your nervous system sounding a false alarm — but your body’s sweat, tears and racing pulse are very real.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a news article about Anandita Dutta Tamuly eating 51 ghost chilies for a Guinness World Record, then discuss the history, heat level, and possible health benefits and risks of chilies.
counterfactuals.output:
# Indian Woman Eats 51 Ghost Chilies in Record-Setting Display

**JORHAT, India —** Anandita Dutta Tamuly stunned spectators in 2009 by eating 51 ghost chilies in two minutes during a Guinness World Records attempt in the northeastern Indian state of Assam.

Tamuly consumed the fiery peppers—known locally as **bhut jolokia**—as celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay watched. She also reportedly rubbed chili seeds into her eyes during the demonstration, an act that underscored her unusual tolerance but carries a serious risk of eye injury.

The feat was widely presented as a Guinness record for the most bhut jolokia peppers eaten in two minutes. Guinness record categories and listings can change, however, so the performance should not necessarily be treated as the current record.

Tamuly, who grew up in Assam, told reporters that she had eaten hot peppers since childhood. Her ability was especially remarkable because the ghost chili was then considered one of the hottest peppers in the world.

## From ancient crop to global seasoning

Chili peppers originated in the Americas and were domesticated thousands of years ago. After European voyages brought them into global trade in the late 15th and 16th centuries, chilies spread rapidly through Africa and Asia.

They became deeply embedded in Indian cooking, even though they were not native to the subcontinent. Farmers in northeastern India developed and preserved exceptionally pungent varieties, including bhut jolokia, whose name is often translated as “ghost pepper.”

## How hot is a ghost chili?

Pepper heat is commonly measured in **Scoville Heat Units**, or SHU, which estimate the concentration of pungent capsaicinoids. A jalapeño generally ranges from about **2,500 to 8,000 SHU**, while ghost chilies commonly test around **800,000 to more than 1 million SHU**, depending on genetics and growing conditions.

Bhut jolokia was recognized by Guinness World Records as the world’s hottest chili in 2007. It has since been surpassed by selectively bred peppers, including the Carolina Reaper and Pepper X.

The burning sensation comes mainly from **capsaicin**, which activates the body’s TRPV1 receptors—the same sensory system involved in detecting damaging heat. Capsaicin does not literally raise the mouth’s temperature, but the nervous system interprets the signal as intense burning.

## Possible health benefits

Chilies can be part of a nutritious diet. They contain vitamin C, carotenoids and other plant compounds, although cooking and portion size affect how much is consumed.

Research suggests capsaicin may:

- Briefly increase energy expenditure and reduce appetite in some people  
- Help relieve certain types of nerve or joint pain when used in regulated topical medicines  
- Produce modest cardiovascular or metabolic benefits when chili-rich foods are eaten as part of an overall healthy diet  

Observational studies have linked regular chili consumption with lower rates of death from some causes, but these findings do not prove that chilies themselves are responsible. Lifestyle, diet and cultural factors may also explain the association.

## Risks of extreme chili consumption

Eating a normal culinary amount is generally safe for most adults, but extreme quantities can cause intense mouth and throat pain, sweating, tearing, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhea. In rare cases, very hot peppers have been associated with serious complications such as esophageal injury after forceful vomiting, severe headaches, breathing problems or dangerous cardiovascular stress.

Capsaicin can also badly irritate the skin and eyes. Anyone handling superhot peppers should wear gloves, avoid touching the face and wash exposed areas carefully. An eye exposed to chili should be flushed with clean, lukewarm water; persistent pain or vision changes require urgent medical attention.

Milk or yogurt may soothe mouth pain better than water because milk proteins and fat can help disperse capsaicin. Competitive chili-eating—and especially placing pepper material in the eyes—should not be imitated.

Tamuly’s performance remains a dramatic illustration of human tolerance and northeastern India’s chili culture. For most people, however, ghost peppers are best approached as a potent seasoning rather than a test of endurance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain why chilies feel painfully hot and how capsaicinoids affect the human body. Compare ghost peppers with Tabasco sauce and jalapeños using Scoville units.
counterfactuals.output:
Chilies feel hot because they contain **capsaicinoids**, especially **capsaicin** and **dihydrocapsaicin**. These chemicals bind to **TRPV1 receptors** on pain-sensing nerves—the same receptors activated by damaging heat, acidity, and inflammation. The brain therefore receives a “burning” signal even though the chili has not actually raised tissue temperature.

### Effects on the body
Capsaicinoid exposure can cause:

- Burning pain in the mouth, skin, or eyes
- Salivation, tearing, runny nose, coughing, and sweating
- Flushing and a temporary rise in heart rate
- Stomach discomfort, cramps, vomiting, or diarrhea at high doses

The body may also release endorphins in response to the pain. With repeated exposure, TRPV1 nerves become less responsive, producing tolerance. This desensitizing effect is why concentrated capsaicin is used in topical treatments for certain types of nerve and joint pain.

Capsaicin usually causes irritation rather than a true thermal burn, although very concentrated exposure can produce intense inflammation and, rarely, serious complications.

### Scoville comparison

| Food or sauce | Approximate heat |
|---|---:|
| Jalapeño pepper | **2,500–8,000 SHU** |
| Original Tabasco sauce | **2,500–5,000 SHU** |
| Ghost pepper (*Bhut jolokia*) | **About 800,000–1,041,000 SHU** |

**SHU** means **Scoville Heat Units**, a measure of capsaicinoid concentration. Thus, a ghost pepper can be roughly **100–400 times hotter** than a jalapeño or original Tabasco sauce, depending on the particular peppers and batches. Tabasco sauce is milder than the raw peppers used to make it because they are diluted with vinegar and other ingredients.

counterfactuals.output:
# How chilies affect the body

In 2009, in Jorhat, Assam, Indian chili enthusiast Anandita Dutta Tamuly reportedly ate 51 bhut jolokia—“ghost chilies”—in two minutes while celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay watched. She then rubbed seeds from the peppers into her eyes, apparently without visible distress. The record-setting exhibition was especially remarkable because the bhut jolokia was among the first peppers measured at more than one million Scoville heat units—hundreds of times hotter than a typical jalapeño (Bosland and Baral, 2007).

Most people would react very differently. A ghost chili can provoke searing pain, sweating, tears, coughing, a racing heart and gastrointestinal distress. Yet the chili is not literally burning tissue in the way a flame does. Its principal pungent chemical, capsaicin, activates the body’s heat- and pain-sensing machinery.

## An ancient human taste

Chili peppers belong to the genus *Capsicum* and originated in the Americas. Archaeological evidence—including microscopic starch grains recovered from cooking vessels and tools—indicates that people were using domesticated chilies more than 6,000 years ago in parts of Central and South America (Perry et al., 2007). Genetic and ecological research suggests that *Capsicum annuum*, the species that includes jalapeños, cayenne and many sweet peppers, was domesticated in Mexico (Kraft et al., 2014).

After Columbus’s voyages, chilies traveled rapidly through European, African and Asian trade networks. Portuguese merchants helped introduce them to India during the 16th century. They became so deeply embedded in Indian cooking that it is easy to forget they were a relatively recent arrival.

The bhut jolokia is associated particularly with northeastern India. It is generally classified within *Capsicum chinense*, although regional varieties may show evidence of complex ancestry. In a 2007 study, horticulturists Paul Bosland and Jit Baral reported an average heat level of 1,001,304 Scoville heat units, confirming its then-extraordinary pungency.

## Why chilies feel hot

Capsaicin binds to transient receptor potential vanilloid 1, or **TRPV1**, a protein found on sensory nerve endings. TRPV1 normally responds to potentially damaging heat, acidity and certain inflammatory signals. Its role as the capsaicin receptor was established in landmark experiments by David Julius and colleagues (Caterina et al., 1997).

When capsaicin activates TRPV1 in the mouth, the nerves send a warning to the brain that resembles the signal produced by excessive heat. The brain therefore interprets the chemical stimulus as burning pain even though the chili has not raised the mouth to a scalding temperature.

The body responds as though it needs to cool and protect itself:

- Blood vessels in the skin may dilate, causing flushing.
- Sweat production increases.
- The eyes water and the nose runs.
- Saliva and mucus production may rise.
- Breathing and heart rate can briefly accelerate.
- Endogenous pain-control systems, including endorphin-related pathways, may be recruited.

This combination of pain, excitement and relief helps explain why some people find very hot food pleasurable.

## Why tolerance develops

Repeated chili consumption can make the same dose feel less intense. Persistent TRPV1 stimulation temporarily makes sensory neurons less responsive, a process often described as desensitization. Cultural familiarity and learned expectations also matter: experienced chili eaters are generally better able to interpret and tolerate the sensation.

Desensitization does not make a person invulnerable. Someone who appears comfortable may still develop irritation, vomiting or diarrhea after a sufficiently large dose. Individual sensitivity also varies greatly, so a quantity tolerated by one person can overwhelm another.

The same desensitizing effect has medical uses. Topical capsaicin creams and high-concentration patches are used for certain forms of neuropathic pain. Initial application may burn, but continued or concentrated exposure can reduce the activity of pain-signaling nerve fibers. Clinical uses include some cases of postherpetic neuralgia and other localized neuropathic pain conditions.

## Effects on the stomach and intestines

After swallowing, capsaicin activates sensory receptors throughout the gastrointestinal tract. Common short-term effects include:

- Abdominal burning or cramping
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Faster intestinal movement
- Painful diarrhea or a burning sensation during defecation

Spicy food does not automatically cause an ulcer. Most peptic ulcers are linked to *Helicobacter pylori* infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and aspirin. Some laboratory research has even suggested that capsaicin can stimulate protective gastric responses. Nevertheless, chilies can aggravate symptoms in people with reflux, functional dyspepsia, irritable bowel syndrome or existing gastrointestinal inflammation.

Capsaicin is fat-soluble, which is why water does little to remove it from the mouth. Dairy products can be more effective: milk fat helps dissolve capsaicin, while the milk protein casein can help dislodge it from oral surfaces. Oils and starchy foods may also provide some relief.

## Metabolism and appetite

Capsaicin can modestly increase thermogenesis—the production of heat—and may slightly raise energy expenditure or fat oxidation. Controlled trials and reviews have also found small effects on appetite in some participants. However, the changes are generally too limited and inconsistent to make chilies a stand-alone weight-loss treatment (Ludy, Moore and Mattes, 2012; Whiting et al., 2012).

Regular chili eaters may experience weaker metabolic effects because tolerance develops. The form and dose matter as well: eating a pepper as part of a meal is not equivalent to taking a standardized capsaicinoid supplement.

## Possible long-term health associations

Large observational studies have linked frequent spicy-food consumption with lower overall mortality and, in some populations, lower rates of cardiovascular or respiratory death. For example, a prospective Chinese cohort study published in *The BMJ* found that people who reported eating spicy foods six or seven days a week had a lower risk of death during follow-up than those eating them less than once a week (Lv et al., 2015).

Such findings do not prove that chilies themselves prolong life. Chili consumption may accompany other dietary, social or lifestyle factors, and observational studies cannot eliminate all confounding. Researchers have proposed several possible mechanisms—including effects on blood-vessel function, inflammation, gut microbes and glucose regulation—but clinical evidence remains incomplete.

The most defensible conclusion is that chilies can fit comfortably within a healthy diet for people who tolerate them. Claims that capsaicin prevents cancer, cures metabolic disease or causes dramatic weight loss go beyond the available human evidence.

## Can extreme chilies be dangerous?

Ordinary culinary use is generally safe, but extreme exposures can cause medical emergencies. Very hot peppers and concentrated extracts have been associated in case reports with severe vomiting, chest pain, esophageal injury and intense headaches. Rarely, extreme chili challenges have been followed by reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, in which brain arteries temporarily narrow and cause sudden “thunderclap” headaches.

Capsaicin in the eyes produces severe pain, tearing and involuntary eyelid closure. Eyes should be flushed promptly with plenty of clean water or saline, and contact lenses should be removed. Persistent eye pain or visual disturbance requires medical evaluation. Skin contamination should be handled carefully, ideally with gloves; touching the face after preparing superhot peppers can transfer a surprisingly potent dose.

A person should seek urgent medical help after chili exposure if there is difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, fainting, confusion, uncontrollable vomiting, blood in vomit or stool, severe abdominal pain, or a sudden extreme headache.

## Heat, pain and culture

The ghost-chili feat witnessed by Gordon Ramsay illustrates both the potency of capsaicin and the extraordinary range of human tolerance. Chilies trigger an ancient biological alarm system, convincing sensory nerves that the body is confronting dangerous heat. In moderate amounts, that alarm can be enjoyable and may have modest physiological effects. At extreme doses, however, it can produce genuine injury and medical risk.

Humans have cultivated chilies for thousands of years not despite the pain, but partly because of it: the burn creates flavor, excitement, ritual and identity. Capsaicin turns eating into a controlled encounter with danger—and, for most diners, one that ends when the meal does.

### Selected research

- Bosland, P. W., and Baral, J. B. (2007). “Bhut Jolokia”—The world’s hottest known chile pepper is a putative naturally occurring interspecific hybrid. *HortScience*, 42(2), 222–224.  
- Caterina, M. J., et al. (1997). The capsaicin receptor: A heat-activated ion channel in the pain pathway. *Nature*, 389, 816–824.  
- Kraft, K. H., et al. (2014). Multiple lines of evidence for the origin of domesticated chili pepper, *Capsicum annuum*, in Mexico. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 111(17), 6165–6170.  
- Ludy, M.-J., Moore, G. E., and Mattes, R. D. (2012). The effects of capsaicin and capsiate on energy balance. *Chemical Senses*, 37(2), 103–121.  
- Lv, J., et al. (2015). Consumption of spicy foods and total and cause-specific mortality: Population-based cohort study. *The BMJ*, 351, h3942.  
- Perry, L., et al. (2007). Starch fossils and the domestication and dispersal of chili peppers in the Americas. *Science*, 315(5814), 986–988.  
- Whiting, S., Derbyshire, E., and Tiwari, B. K. (2012). Capsaicinoids and capsinoids: A potential role for weight management? *Appetite*, 59(2), 341–348.

counterfactuals.output:
# Chili Peppers: The Fruit That Tricks the Brain, Cools the Body, and Challenges the Stomach

A chili pepper does not actually burn human tissue—at least not in the way a hot stove does. Instead, it performs a remarkably convincing chemical illusion. Its principal pungent compounds, the capsaicinoids, activate sensory machinery normally used to detect potentially damaging heat. The brain receives a warning signal, the eyes water, blood vessels widen, sweat appears, and the heart may beat faster. Yet the pepper itself may be at room temperature.

That sensory trick helps explain both the enduring appeal of chilies and the extraordinary number of health claims attached to them. Over thousands of years, chili peppers have served as foods, medicines, preservatives, ritual objects, and tests of courage. Modern research supports some of their traditional uses, weakens others, and leaves several important questions unresolved.

## An ancient American crop that conquered the world

Chili peppers belong to the genus *Capsicum*, which originated in the Americas. Archaeological and genetic evidence indicates that Indigenous peoples were gathering, using, and eventually domesticating wild peppers thousands of years ago. Different species were domesticated in different regions: *Capsicum annuum*, the species that includes jalapeños, cayenne peppers, bell peppers, and many other familiar varieties, was domesticated in Mexico, while other species developed important cultivation histories in South America and the Caribbean.

Evidence from ancient starch grains, seeds, and plant remains suggests that chilies were part of American cuisines at least six millennia ago, and probably earlier in some places. They were valued not simply for heat but for flavor, color, food preservation, trade, ritual, and medicine.

The global spread came after European contact with the Americas in the late 15th century. Portuguese and Spanish trade networks carried peppers into Africa, Europe, India, China, and Southeast Asia. Chilies grew readily in warm climates and offered a relatively inexpensive way to add intensity to food. Within a few centuries, a plant unknown outside the Americas had become so deeply embedded in cuisines from Sichuan to South India and Ethiopia that it can now seem indigenous to them.

## Why chilies feel hot

Capsaicin is the best-known pungent molecule in chili peppers, although several related capsaicinoids contribute to their heat. These compounds are concentrated mainly in the pale internal tissue—the placenta—to which the seeds attach. The seeds themselves are not major capsaicin factories, but their surfaces become coated through contact.

Capsaicin binds to TRPV1, a protein found on pain-sensing nerve endings. TRPV1 normally responds to damaging heat, acidity, and certain inflammatory signals. When capsaicin switches it on, the nervous system interprets the result as burning.

This is why drinking water provides little relief: capsaicin is oily and poorly soluble in water. Water may simply spread it around the mouth. Foods containing fat or proteins—milk and yogurt, for example—can help remove it more effectively. Repeated exposure can also make the receptors and nerve fibers temporarily less responsive, producing the familiar phenomenon of chili tolerance.

The Scoville scale, traditionally based on how much a pepper extract had to be diluted before tasters could no longer detect its heat, reflects capsaicinoid concentration. Modern laboratories can measure these chemicals directly. Sweet bell peppers score essentially zero, while the hottest cultivars can exceed a million Scoville heat units.

## From folk medicine to pain patches

Chilies acquired medicinal reputations wherever they were adopted. Traditional systems have used them to stimulate appetite, warm the body, clear congestion, improve circulation, aid digestion, or treat pain. Not all such claims have survived scientific testing, but one apparently paradoxical use has: capsaicin can relieve pain.

At first, capsaicin excites pain-sensing nerves. With repeated or sustained exposure, however, those nerve endings become less responsive. Topical capsaicin creams and high-concentration patches are therefore used for some forms of neuropathic pain, including pain following shingles and certain diabetic nerve problems. The treatment can itself cause substantial burning, especially at first, and high-dose patches are generally applied under medical supervision.

Researchers have also studied capsaicin for arthritis pain, itching, nasal symptoms, and other conditions. Evidence and product quality vary. Eating very hot food is not equivalent to applying a standardized medical preparation, and chilies should not be treated as a substitute for proven care.

## Can eating chilies cool you down?

Oddly enough, chilies can contribute to cooling—under the right conditions.

By activating heat-sensitive nerves, capsaicin persuades the brain that the body is overheating. The response may include sweating and widening of blood vessels near the skin. If sweat evaporates, it carries heat away. This may help explain why pungent foods are common in many hot climates.

But sweating is not automatically cooling. In humid air, where evaporation is limited, sweat may merely leave a person wet and uncomfortable. A very spicy meal can also create a strong subjective sensation of heat before any evaporative cooling occurs. Chilies therefore do not lower body temperature like an air conditioner; they provoke a physiological response that *can* increase heat loss.

## The chili “high”: pain, reward, and endorphins

Many chili enthusiasts describe a rush, glow, or mild euphoria after eating exceptionally hot food. A popular explanation is that the brain releases endorphins—endogenous opioid molecules—in response to pain. Stress hormones and other neurotransmitter systems may also contribute, as may excitement, expectation, and the social drama of taking on a culinary challenge.

The broad idea is plausible: painful and stressful stimuli can activate the body’s pain-control and reward pathways. But the neat story that “capsaicin causes a precisely measured endorphin high” is often stated more confidently than the human evidence allows. The experience probably reflects several processes at once: pain signaling, relief when the pain fades, learned enjoyment, adrenaline-like arousal, and social context.

Chili liking also demonstrates how perception can be trained. What begins as an aversive sensation may become “benign masochism”—the enjoyment of an alarm response while knowing one is actually safe.

## Digestion: stimulant, irritant, or both?

Chilies have a complicated relationship with the digestive system.

Capsaicin can stimulate saliva and gastric secretions and alter gut sensation and motility. Some people believe spicy food helps them digest a heavy meal. Others develop burning pain, cramps, reflux symptoms, or diarrhea. Both experiences can be genuine because individual sensitivity, dose, tolerance, and underlying illness vary widely.

Contrary to an old belief, spicy food is not considered a primary cause of peptic ulcers. Most ulcers result from infection with *Helicobacter pylori* or from drugs such as aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines. Capsaicin does not literally burn a hole in the stomach. Experimental work has even suggested that modest exposure can stimulate protective mechanisms in the gastric lining.

That does not mean chilies are harmless to everyone. They can worsen symptoms in some people with gastroesophageal reflux, functional dyspepsia, irritable bowel syndrome, anal fissures, or an already inflamed digestive tract. Capsaicin may remain active as it travels through the gut, accounting for the notorious “second burn” during defecation. Anyone who consistently experiences symptoms has a better guide than broad dietary folklore: their own reproducible response, discussed with a clinician when symptoms are severe or persistent.

## Do chilies speed metabolism or cause weight loss?

Capsaicin can modestly increase thermogenesis—the production of heat—and may temporarily raise energy expenditure and fat oxidation. It may also reduce appetite in some experimental settings. Non-pungent capsaicin-related compounds called capsinoids have been investigated for similar effects.

The key word is *modestly*. Studies are often short, doses vary, tolerance may develop, and the extra calories burned are generally too few to produce dramatic weight loss on their own. A chili-rich diet can support weight management if it makes nutritious foods satisfying without adding much energy. It can do the opposite if the chili arrives in deep-fried food, sugary sauce, or a large high-calorie meal.

Capsaicin is therefore an interesting metabolic signal, not a fat-melting shortcut. Overall diet, physical activity, sleep, medication, health conditions, and food environment matter much more.

## Small fruit, useful nutrients

Fresh chilies can be highly nutritious. Depending on variety and ripeness, they provide:

- Vitamin C, sometimes in strikingly high concentrations  
- Provitamin A carotenoids, especially in red and orange peppers  
- Vitamin B6 and smaller amounts of other B vitamins  
- Vitamin K, potassium, and other minerals  
- Fiber  
- Pigments and polyphenols with antioxidant activity  

Red peppers generally contain more mature carotenoid pigments than green ones. Dried chili powders concentrate some nutrients but may lose vitamin C during drying and storage. They can also contribute significant sodium when sold in seasoning blends.

A practical limitation is serving size. A pepper may be nutrient-dense, but someone who eats only a pinch of chili powder receives much less nutrition than someone eating a full sweet pepper. Chilies can enrich a diet, but they do not compensate for a lack of varied fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, and other nutritious foods.

## The stomach-cancer controversy

The relationship between chili consumption and stomach cancer has attracted concern because some observational studies—particularly in populations with very high chili intake—have reported higher rates of gastric or other gastrointestinal cancers. Other studies have found no clear association or have suggested lower overall mortality among people who regularly eat spicy foods.

These findings are difficult to interpret. People who eat large amounts of chili may differ in many other ways: salt intake, food preservation methods, smoking, alcohol use, poverty, access to refrigeration and health care, genetic background, and rates of *H. pylori* infection. Some chili products may also be contaminated with molds, adulterants, or other carcinogenic substances during poor storage or processing. Reverse causation and inaccurate dietary reporting further complicate the picture.

Laboratory research is equally complex. At different concentrations and in different experimental systems, capsaicin has shown both potentially anticancer effects—such as promoting the death of abnormal cells—and potentially harmful effects, including irritation and promotion of inflammation. A result in isolated cells or rodents does not establish what ordinary human consumption does over decades.

The most defensible conclusion is that moderate chili intake has not been proven to cause stomach cancer. At the same time, very high habitual intake cannot be declared risk-free on current evidence, especially when combined with established hazards. Reducing stomach-cancer risk should focus on better-supported measures: detecting and treating *H. pylori* when appropriate, not smoking, limiting heavily salted and preserved foods, moderating alcohol, maintaining a healthy diet, and seeking medical attention for persistent symptoms such as unexplained weight loss, vomiting, anemia, difficulty swallowing, or gastrointestinal bleeding.

## Chilies and the cardiovascular system

Capsaicin’s activation of TRPV1 can affect blood vessels, nerve signals, inflammation, and metabolism. Small trials and animal studies suggest possible improvements in vascular function, blood pressure regulation, cholesterol handling, glucose control, and platelet activity. Eating chilies may also help people use less salt by making food taste more vivid—a potentially valuable indirect effect.

Large observational studies have sometimes linked regular chili or spicy-food consumption with lower rates of cardiovascular death and lower total mortality. These results are intriguing but do not prove that chilies caused the benefit. Chili eaters may have different overall diets, activity levels, cultural habits, or socioeconomic circumstances. “Spicy food” also means very different things across populations.

Acute responses deserve mention. A very hot meal can temporarily increase heart rate, sweating, and skin blood flow. For most healthy people this is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, but extreme chili challenges can provoke vomiting, severe headaches, chest pain, or marked blood-pressure changes. Rare case reports have described serious complications, often after exceptionally concentrated exposure. People with cardiovascular disease should not regard a chili-eating contest as a health intervention.

Nor should capsaicin supplements replace prescribed blood-pressure or cholesterol treatment. Supplements can deliver doses unlike those found in ordinary meals and may interact with medicines or aggravate gastrointestinal symptoms.

## A food, not a miracle drug

Chili peppers occupy a fascinating boundary between pleasure and pain. Their chemistry activates an ancient warning system, yet humans have turned that warning into cuisine. They may encourage sweating, provoke a stress-and-reward response, supply useful nutrients, and produce modest metabolic effects. Capsaicin also has a genuine medical role in certain topical pain treatments.

But the broader health story resists simple labels. Chilies do not cause ulcers in the traditional sense, yet they can aggravate digestive symptoms. They may fit into a heart-healthy diet, but cardiovascular benefits remain largely associative. Moderate intake has not been shown to cause stomach cancer, though questions remain about very high exposure and the context in which chilies are consumed. Their effect on body weight is real enough to study but far too small to replace established weight-management strategies.

For most people, the sensible approach is culinary rather than pharmacological: eat chilies in amounts that are enjoyable and tolerable, use them to add flavor to nutritious foods, and do not mistake intensity for therapeutic power. The pepper’s greatest achievement may not be that it cures disease, but that a plant once confined to the Americas persuaded much of the world to enjoy the sensation of being on fire.
